items.parentTitle: Odd and Even Numbers and Divisibility Rules
items.whatStudentsLearn: In Level 3 Mathematics, children identify, explain, and use the properties of odd and even numbers, exploring patterns in addition, subtraction, and multiplication.
items.whatThisMeans: Even numbers can be divided into two equal groups with nothing left over (ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8), while odd numbers always have 1 left over (ending in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). Adding two even numbers always gives an even number.
items.whyItMatters: Recognising parity (odd vs even) provides an instant sanity check for mental arithmetic calculations and introduces divisibility logic.

homeActivities.title: Pairing Snack Challenge
homeActivities.description: Give your child a handful of crackers or grapes. Ask them to pair them up by twos to discover if the starting total was odd or even.

items.parentTitle: Reading, Writing, and Ordering Numbers Beyond 10,000
items.whatStudentsLearn: In Level 3 Mathematics, children recognise, represent, and order numbers beyond 10,000 using standard place value conventions, renaming numbers flexibly into ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones.
items.whatThisMeans: Understanding how digits work in 5-digit numbers (like 24,580). The repeating cycle of ones, tens, hundreds, and thousands helps children read large numbers like sports crowd sizes or suburb populations.
items.whyItMatters: Place value mastery is the foundation for multidigit arithmetic, financial numeracy, and metric measurement conversions.

homeActivities.title: The Car Odometer Challenge
homeActivities.description: Look at car odometers, house prices in real estate windows, or stadium attendance numbers. Ask: 'What digit is in the ten-thousands place? What is that digit worth?'

items.whatStudentsLearn: Children recognise and represent unit fractions (such as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/10) and their multiples using diagrams and number lines, combining fractions with the same denominator to make a whole.
items.whatThisMeans: Understanding that fractions are equal parts of one whole object or collection. For example, 4 quarters (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4) make one whole pizza.
items.whyItMatters: Fractions build essential proportional reasoning needed for cooking measurements, time reading, and decimals.

homeActivities.title: Pizza and Sandwich Fraction Cutting
homeActivities.description: Cut a sandwich or pancake into 4 equal quarters or 5 equal strips. Have your child show how many pieces are needed to make 1/2 or the whole sandwich.

items.parentTitle: Mental and Written Addition and Subtraction (2- and 3-Digit)
items.whatStudentsLearn: Students add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value partitioning, regrouping, and mental jump strategies without relying on calculators.
items.whatThisMeans: Breaking numbers into easy pieces to calculate mentally (e.g. adding 145 + 38 by doing 145 + 30 = 175, then 175 + 8 = 183).
items.whyItMatters: Mental computation fluency builds confidence with everyday shopping budgets and multi-step word problems.

homeActivities.title: Shopping Receipt Round-Up
homeActivities.description: Pick two items from a supermarket receipt (e.g. $1.40 and $2.30). Ask your child to add the totals mentally using tens and ones.

items.whatStudentsLearn: Students recognise the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction, applying it to solve number sentences with missing values (e.g. __ + 14 = 30).
items.whatThisMeans: Knowing that addition and subtraction undo each other. If 15 + 7 = 22, then 22 - 7 must equal 15.
items.whyItMatters: Foundational principle of algebraic problem solving, balance equations, and checking calculations.

homeActivities.title: Fact Family Triangles
homeActivities.description: Write three numbers like 8, 12, and 20 at the corners of a triangle. Challenge your child to state two addition and two subtraction sentences using those numbers.

items.parentTitle: Measuring and Estimating with Metric Units
items.whatStudentsLearn: Children identify standard metric units (millimetres, centimetres, metres, grams, kilograms, millilitres, litres) and use familiar benchmarks to make sensible estimates.
items.whatThisMeans: Knowing that a door is about 2 metres tall, a milk bottle holds 1 or 2 litres, and an apple weighs about 150 grams.
items.whyItMatters: Estimating and measuring accurately is used continuously in cooking, sports, carpentry, and science.

homeActivities.title: Kitchen Metric Scale Guess
homeActivities.description: Hold a can of soup and estimate its weight in grams, then check the label or weigh it on kitchen scales to see how close you were.

items.parentTitle: Comparing and Classifying 3D Objects by Geometric Features
items.whatStudentsLearn: Students make, compare, and classify 3D objects (prisms, cylinders, cones, pyramids), explaining how their faces, edges, and vertices suit them for particular purposes.
items.whatThisMeans: Explaining why wheels and cans are cylinders (they roll), while building bricks and shipping containers are rectangular prisms (they stack safely).
items.whyItMatters: Spatial visual reasoning is essential for engineering, robotics, architecture, and design.

homeActivities.title: Pantry Packaging Architect
homeActivities.description: Examine food packages in your pantry. Ask your child which shapes can stack on top of each other and which cannot, explaining why based on flat vs curved surfaces.

items.parentTitle: Collecting Survey Data and Reading Column Graphs
items.whatStudentsLearn: Children conduct simple surveys, record categorical data in tally tables, and create column graphs and picture graphs with one-to-one and many-to-one scales.
items.whatThisMeans: Organising information so patterns stand out clearly, such as showing which pet or sport is most popular in a group.
items.whyItMatters: Data literacy enables children to interpret charts, science findings, and news media accurately.

homeActivities.title: Family Favorite Meal Survey
homeActivities.description: Have your child survey family members on their favorite dinner and draw a neat column graph showing the result.

items.parentTitle: Conducting Chance Experiments and Probability Language
items.whatStudentsLearn: In Level 3, Probability is introduced as a standalone strand. Students conduct chance experiments (flipping coins, rolling dice) and describe outcomes using probability terms like 'certain', 'likely', 'equal chance', 'unlikely', and 'impossible'.
items.whatThisMeans: Learning to evaluate likelihood. It is 'certain' tomorrow will have a sunrise, 'equal chance' to flip heads or tails, and 'impossible' to roll a 9 on a 6-sided die.
items.whyItMatters: Builds rational thinking about risk, games, and foundational statistics.

homeActivities.title: Board Game Die Tracker
homeActivities.description: Roll a die 12 times during a family board game. Keep a tally to see if every number appeared roughly equally.
